pairs.rationale: Both foreground Christ crucified in the proclamation addressed to communities. Corinthians names its reception as stumbling block or foolishness; Galatians asks who bewitched the readers after Christ's public portrayal. The source does not identify the portrayal's medium or say these readers physically witnessed the crucifixion.

Acts narrates the Holy Spirit falling on people while they hear Peter's message. It is a concrete hearing/Spirit-reception comparison for Paul's works-of-law or hearing-with-faith question. Acts does not reproduce the question or identify its hearers as the Galatians.

Both contrast Spirit and flesh in the believers' life. Galatians questions a move from beginning by Spirit to being completed by flesh; Romans contrasts walking and setting the mind according to each. The question's stages and Romans' life/peace/death consequences remain distinct.

The letter later expresses fear of laboring over the readers in vain. That is an internal counterpart to this question about suffering in vain: the sufferers' experience and the minister's labor have different subjects, and if-indeed preserves the uncertainty rather than declaring either experience finally wasted.

The Spirit/faith/acts-of-power cluster also appears in Corinthians' gift list. Galatians asks about the One supplying Spirit and power; Corinthians names faith, healings and acts of power distributed by the one Spirit. The unnamed supplier, named Spirit and hearing-faith/gift-of-faith roles are not flattened.

The believed-God and righteousness-reckoning sentence closely corresponds to Genesis. Galatians calls him Abraham and says credited; the actual Genesis unit calls him Abram and says reckoned. Genesis17:5 explicitly supplies the name change, rather than editing the earlier target name to match.

Romans describes Abraham as father of believing uncircumcised people and of circumcised people walking in his earlier faith. This corresponds to faith-based Abrahamic sonship here, while the father/sons expressions and circumcision-specific explanation retain their actual differences.

The in-you blessing formula corresponds to Genesis12:3, but Genesis says all the tribes of the earth, where Galatians says all the nations. Foreseeing faith-justification and gospel-beforehand language are Paul's stated interpretation, not additional sentences placed in Genesis.

Both connect Abraham's faith with benefits shared by believing people. Galatians names blessing with believing Abraham; Romans names faith, grace and a secure promise for the seed and calls him father of us all. The blessing and promise descriptions are related rather than identical clauses.

The curse on not continuing in all the law's requirements closely corresponds to Deuteronomy. Galatians has things written in the law's book; Deuteronomy has words of this law and the people's So be it. Paul's application to those of works of law is not added to the quoted law as an identical unconditional sentence.

The righteous-one/living formula corresponds to Habakkuk, but the supplied target says by My faithfulness rather than Galatians' by faith. Habakkuk also has the preceding drawing-back and My-soul clause. Those actual words are preserved without silently changing the possessor or equating every expression.

Leviticus gives the do-them/live-by-them clause after naming God's ordinances and judgments. Galatians uses that clause in its own law/faith contrast; the target does not itself state the introductory law-is-not-of-faith proposition or omit its divine self-identification.

The tree-hanging curse directly corresponds to Deuteronomy's death-and-burial rule. The target says cursed by God and includes burial that day; Galatians' shorter citation omits that phrase and applies the curse to Christ buying us free. That interpretation is not represented as Christ explicitly named in Deuteronomy.

Acts explicitly reports the Spirit's gift poured upon Gentile hearers, with Peter acknowledging their receipt before ordering water baptism in the context. That corresponds to the nations receiving Spirit in this blessing argument. Abraham, promise and through-faith wording remain Galatians' own explanation rather than an identical Acts sentence.

The later God-ratified-covenant statement applies this ratification analogy to the promise and a subsequent law. The comparison follows the explicit human-terms example and its application, without asserting a contemporary legal rule or inventing an actual human estate behind the analogy.

Genesis promises land to you and to your seed; Galatians identifies the quoted singular seed with Christ. Genesis' next verse also compares the seed with earth's sand. The target's land and collective-family context remain visible rather than claiming Genesis names Christ or every singular seed must be one individual.

Genesis explicitly records the Lord making a covenant with Abram and promising land to his seed. This supplies concrete background for a previously God-ratified covenant/promise, without inserting the later law or a four-hundred-thirty-year calculation into the Genesis sentence.

Exodus gives four hundred thirty years for Israel's residence in Egypt and Canaan before departure; Galatians gives that interval for the law coming after the earlier covenant. It is specific Exodus-period chronological background, preserving the different stated endpoints without claiming an independent law-giving date or silently removing Canaan.

Both oppose deriving Abraham's inheritance or heirship from law rather than promise and faith. Romans specifies heir of the world and the nullified-promise consequence; Galatians emphasizes God's gracious giving through promise. The objects and conditional formulations are kept distinct.

Acts speaks of receiving law through angels' ordinances and not keeping it. Galatians describes law ordained through angels by a mediator and gives a transgression/seed limit. Angel-mediated law is the specific correspondence; neither speech's extra accusation, mediator or timing clause is added to the other.

Both place God's oneness beside mediation language. Galatians says a mediator is not for one alone; Timothy's letter names one mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus. These are different uses of one, and the comparison does not identify Galatians' unnamed mediator or impose a complete interpretation of its terse logic.

Both discuss law's inability in relation to divine righteousness. Galatians denies opposition to the promises and gives the condition of a law able to give life; Romans names weakness through flesh and God's sending His Son. Their condition, explanation and Spirit-walk application are preserved rather than calling law itself evil.

Both use confinement under wrong as the setting for a saving benefit. Galatians names Scripture confining everything under sin and the faith-promise given to believers; Romans names God confining all in disobedience for mercy on all. Agents, objects and beneficiaries are not made the same wording or a universal-outcome theory.

The later child-heir analogy depicts constraint under guardians/stewards and childhood enslavement before the appointed time. It develops this guarded-under-law/until-faith pattern internally. The family/legal image and elements wording remain different from the earlier confinement statement.

Romans calls Christ the end of law for righteousness to everyone believing. That corresponds to the law-as-guardian-until-Christ and justification-by-faith connection here. The actual end wording is retained without replacing it with another translation's goal or deriving an unprinted calendar end date.

pairs.relationship: internal transition from constraint to sonship
pairs.rationale: The later sending, redemption and sonship sequence ends with no longer a slave but a son. It provides an internal transition comparison for no longer under a guardian after faith comes. The guardian, slavery and adoption images are linked without becoming one identical legal status or sentence.

Both connect believing with God's familial designation. Galatians says all sons through faith in Christ Jesus; John gives authority to become children to those receiving and believing in His name, with birth from God. Sons/children and the additional birth clauses retain their actual forms.

Both explicitly describe baptism into Christ. Romans adds baptism into His death, burial and a purpose of walking in life's newness; Galatians says those baptized into Christ have put Him on. The clothing and burial images remain distinct rather than one unprinted account of their physical mode.

Romans directly commands putting on the Lord Jesus Christ and adds no provision for fleshly desires. Galatians declares that the baptized have put on Christ. The shared image preserves command versus completed description and the different baptism/desire contexts.

Both set differing social or communal labels within unity in Christ. Colossians adds circumcision, barbarian and Scythian labels; Galatians includes no male and female. The lists and one-in-Christ versus Christ-all/in-all formulas remain distinct, rather than adding the gender phrase to Colossians or making a biological claim.

Romans connects Abrahamic seed and secured promise with faith and grace and calls Abraham father of us all. That is a specific counterpart to belonging to Christ and being Abraham's seed/heirs here. The if-you-belong condition and the different stated grounds remain visible rather than unconditional ancestry for everyone.

The next rather-clause supplies the stated explanation for a child heir's constraint: guardians and stewards until his father's appointed date. This is an internal premise/explanation connection within Paul's analogy, not an assertion about every contemporary child's actual property rights.

The later fullness-of-time sending and redemption sequence supplies the divine application following the father's-appointed-date analogy. It links the stated time-and-transition structure without computing a date or requiring the human guardian arrangement to be identical to God's action.

Colossians also names the elements of the world, asking why people who died to them with Christ submit to decrees. Galatians recalls childhood enslavement under them. The former-status and conditional-death formulations remain distinct, and the elements are not assigned an unprinted physical or personal identity.

Both explicitly describe God sending His Son in a human-condition context. Galatians names woman's birth and being under law at the fullness of time; Romans says likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin. The likeness qualification and each passage's timing, law and sin language are preserved.

Both connect a change from constraint with adoption as sons. Galatians states the Son's redemption of those under law toward adoption; Romans contrasts slavery/fear with receiving adoption's Spirit and its testimony. The redeeming Son and receiving Spirit roles are related rather than identical actions.

Both include Spirit, adoption and the Abba/Father cry. Galatians says because you are sons God sent His Son's Spirit into our hearts, crying; Romans says you received adoption's Spirit in whom we cry. The you/our/we shifts and the stated crying subject remain intact.

Both reason from sonship or childhood to heirship. Galatians says heir through God; Romans says heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, adding the suffering/glory condition. Those actual expressions are not rewritten as one identical title or an omitted through-Christ phrase.

Thessalonians describes turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God. It is a concrete conversion-from-idolatry counterpart to former enslavement to those by nature not gods. The prior not-knowing and reported turning/serving descriptions remain different rather than one community's event.

Both question a return to submission related to the elements of the world. Galatians corrects knowing-God to being-known-by-God and names weak, impoverished elements; Colossians starts if-you-died-with-Christ and lists prohibitions. The conditions and objects are preserved without identifying the exact disputed systems as one event.

Both discuss calendar observance in a Christ-related argument. Galatians reports days, months, seasons and years; Colossians prohibits judging over festival, new moon or Sabbaths and also names food/drink. The lists and report/command forms are not treated as identical or as proof of a particular modern calendar practice.

Both express fear that labor for the recipients may be in vain. Thessalonians describes sending for news because of concern about the tempter and their faith; Galatians voices fear amid its return-to-elements discussion. The specific communities, conditions and reported actions differ.

Both appeal for the readers to become like or imitate Paul, within a parental ministry setting in Corinthians. Galatians adds reciprocal I-became-as-you and you-did-me-no-wrong language. The comparison does not specify an unprinted act behind becoming-like or reconstruct a private offense.

Both describe Paul's ministry with weakness. Galatians makes weakness of flesh the reason for the first proclamation; Corinthians says he was with them in weakness, fear and trembling. Cause versus accompanying condition is retained, without making the locations, occasion or bodily condition one diagnosed illness.

Jesus' reception-of-messengers teaching compares receiving them with receiving Him and the One who sent Him. That corresponds to the Galatians' welcome of Paul as Christ Jesus. The angel-of-God comparison and fleshly trial are additional Galatians details, not proof Paul literally was Christ or an angel.

The earlier description of welcoming rather than despising Paul supplies the recalled positive reception beside the lost-blessedness question and if-possible eye-gift expression. This is an internal former-attitude comparison, not evidence for an eye disease, surgery or a literal transfer of eyes.

Both connect truth-speaking with an adverse audience response. Galatians asks whether telling truth has made the writer an enemy; Jesus in John says because He speaks truth the hearers do not believe. The question, statement, speakers and audiences remain distinct rather than one identical dispute.

pairs.relationship: internal good and bad pursuit contrast
pairs.rationale: The following but-clause explicitly distinguishes good pursuit for a good purpose from the pursuit here aimed at the readers' reciprocal zeal for others. This internal contrast preserves the stated motive and does not identify what shut-you-out excludes them from or condemn all zeal.

Both say the relevant conduct should not depend solely on the writer's presence. Galatians calls it good to be sought zealously for good at all times; Philippians commands continued obedience beyond presence into absence. Being sought and obeying are different actions and roles, not an identical instruction.

Both use a parental ministry image for the writer's relation to the readers. Galatians depicts renewed labor until Christ is formed in them; Corinthians says he became their father in Christ through the good news. The birth-labor and father images are distinct, not literal biological parentage.

Both relate presence/absence to the writer's manner of addressing the community. Galatians wishes for presence and a changed tone because of perplexity; Corinthians explains absent writing to avoid acting sharply when present. Galatians does not state which direction the tone would change or identify the same visit.

The following for-it-is-written statement supplies the Abraham-and-two-sons story appealed to in this hear-the-law question. This is the text's own appeal-and-narrative-citation connection; the ensuing covenant allegory is identified as an interpretation rather than words inserted into Genesis.

Genesis identifies Hagar's son born to Abraham alongside Sarah's Isaac and calls Hagar the slave woman. This supplies the concrete family background for Galatians' two-son contrast. The free-woman designation and ensuing covenant mapping remain Paul's formulations rather than additional Genesis sentences.

Genesis says the Lord acted for Sarah as He had spoken and she bore Isaac at the stated season. That directly supplies the promise-birth narrative used here; according-to-flesh and free/slave contrasts remain Galatians' interpretive labels rather than a Genesis denial of Isaac's bodily birth.

Genesis explicitly identifies Hagar as Sara's Egyptian slave woman and Abram's wife as Sara. It supplies the character background for Paul's stated allegory. The two-covenant, Sinai and slavery-bearing interpretation is not represented as wording of Genesis16:1; Genesis17:15 supplies Sara's later Sarah name.

The preceding sentence explicitly announces an allegorical interpretation and identifies Hagar with the Sinai covenant bearing slavery. It frames the further Arabia/present-Jerusalem correspondence here. This is an internal extension of the declared allegory, not an unprinted biographical or modern political identity.

Hebrews explicitly names heavenly Jerusalem as the living God's city approached with Mount Zion and angels. That corresponds to Jerusalem above here, while free and our mother are Galatians' own predicates. No earthly address or physical itinerary is inferred from either image.

The barren/deserted woman, childbirth cry and greater number of children closely correspond to Isaiah54:1. Galatians places this written passage in its mother/covenant argument; Isaiah adds for-the-Lord-has-spoken. The quotation does not independently identify Isaiah's figure as a named biological mother in Genesis.

Genesis depicts Sarah's promised birth at the season God spoke and names the son Isaac. It supplies the specific promise-child comparison for the readers being like Isaac. The analogy does not make them Isaac's literal siblings or replace the source's you wording with we.

The saved Genesis text says Hagar's son was playing with Isaac, whereas Galatians describes persecution of the Spirit-born by the flesh-born and adds so-now. This records Paul's interpretation and current analogy without changing playing to an explicit Genesis persecution verb or inventing an inner motive.

The expulsion and non-inheritance sentence closely corresponds to Sarah's speech in Genesis. Genesis says my son Isaac, while Galatians says the son of the free woman and intensifies certainly-not. Those formulations and Paul's allegorical use remain distinct rather than a new literal instruction about an identified modern group.

The earlier belong-to-Christ/Abraham's-seed/heirs-of-promise statement supplies an internal family-inheritance counterpart to being children of the free woman. The earlier condition and you wording and this we conclusion remain visible, rather than turning the allegory into an unqualified biological genealogy.
